extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning to write mathematical proofs (introductory proof/logic course)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and standards for constructing clear, correct proofs in elementary mathematics (logic, set theory, quantifiers). Emphasizes strategies (backward reasoning, instantiation), variable discipline, and how to present final written proofs versus scratch work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work backward using rules of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: If your goal is Q and you have a given P → Q, consider proving P instead and then apply modus ponens to reach Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat antecedents of useful conditional givens as subgoals; add the antecedent to your goal list and try to prove it. Example: goal Q and given P → Q suggests change goal to P; after proving P add one more step to get Q. This is a standard backward-reasoning tactic (illustrated in Example 3.2.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexpress negative givens as equivalent positive statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert negative or difference-style givens into logically equivalent positive/conditional forms that are more useful for reaching the goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use definitions and logical equivalences (e.g., set difference: a ∉ B \ C means ¬(a ∈ B ∧ a ∉ C) ≡ a ∉ B ∨ a ∈ C, which can be rewritten as a ∈ B → a ∈ C). Rewriting negatives often reveals a conditional you can use with modus ponens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the conditional-given strategy (add antecedent to givens)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a conditional statement (P → Q), assume P (add antecedent to givens) and prove Q as the goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a goal is a conditional, change the goal to its consequent and add the antecedent to givens; then proceed to prove the consequent under that assumption. Final proofs often begin 'Suppose P' for this reason (see Example 3.3.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving universal statements by arbitrary element
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∀x P(x), let x be an arbitrary object (a new variable) and prove P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: x must be a new variable not already used to denote a particular object in the proof. Do not assume anything about x other than what you explicitly state. After proving P(x) for an arbitrary x, conclude ∀x P(x). The textbook shows canonical form: 'Let x be arbitrary. [Proof of P(x)]. Since x was arbitrary, ∀x P(x).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce fresh variables when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If a variable name is already used to denote a particular object, choose a new unused variable (e.g., y) when you need an arbitrary variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reusing variable names to prevent accidental assumptions about identity. The book emphasizes choosing a different variable if the letter is already in use, e.g., replace ∀x P(x) with ∀y P(y) and let y be arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving universally quantified implications (∀x(P(x)→Q(x)))
rubrics_metrics.description: Let x be arbitrary and assume P(x); then prove Q(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often proofs begin 'Suppose P(x)' (with the understanding x is arbitrary). Combining the 'arbitrary element' and 'conditional' strategies is the standard approach for such goals (see Examples 3.3.2 and 3.3.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving existential statements by exhibiting a witness
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∃x P(x), choose a particular value for x (a witness), start 'Let x = ...', and prove P(x) for that chosen value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding the witness can involve trial-and-error, solving equations, or other heuristics; the process you used to find the witness belongs in your scratch work and should not be part of the final proof. The final write-up should simply present the chosen witness and verify P(x). Example: solving a quadratic to exhibit y such that y(y+1)=x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential instantiation for given existentials
rubrics_metrics.description: When given ∃x P(x), you may introduce a new name x0 for some particular object satisfying P(x0) and add P(x0) to the givens, but you may not assume anything else about x0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use existential instantiation immediately to name a witness from a given existential if it seems useful. Be careful not to assume properties of x0 beyond P(x0). This is different from proving an existential, where you get to choose the witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal instantiation for given universals
rubrics_metrics.description: When given ∀x P(x), you can substitute any particular object a for x to conclude P(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wait to instantiate until a likely candidate a appears in the proof (e.g., from other givens or constructions). For givens like ∀x(P(x)→Q(x)), instantiate with an a for which you know P(a) (or ¬Q(a) if using backward reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate set-notation givens into logical form and apply instantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret set relations (e.g., A ⊆ B means ∀x(x ∈ A → x ∈ B)) and use universal instantiation and modus ponens as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from A ⊆ B and a ∈ A, infer a ∈ B by instantiating the universal and applying modus ponens. Translating to predicate form helps identify which inference rules to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-chasing for subset proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a subset relation A ⊆ B, let x be an arbitrary element of A and show x ∈ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with a single arbitrary element rather than talking about 'all elements' repeatedly. After showing x ∈ B and noting x was arbitrary, conclude A ⊆ B. This simplifies reasoning and is the canonical method for subset proofs (see Examples 3.3.1 and 3.3.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce variables before use and state what they denote
rubrics_metrics.description: Always tell the reader what newly introduced variables stand for (e.g., 'Let x be an arbitrary element of A', 'Let y = ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to introduce variables causes confusion. Also ensure the type of each variable is clear (number, set, function, matrix, etc.), since notation like a ∈ X only makes sense if X is a set. The book warns that variables must always be introduced before they are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do only as much logical analysis as necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing the logical form of givens and goals to plan a proof, perform only enough translation/expansion to determine the next useful step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-analyzing (expanding every definition immediately) can introduce unnecessary complication. Translate definitions only when they guide the next inference—fill in further details later as needed (illustrated in Example 3.3.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use givens to suggest witnesses or instantiations
rubrics_metrics.description: When the goal requires finding a particular object (e.g., ∃A ∈ G x ∈ A), inspect the givens for candidate objects (e.g., from an existential instantiation) to use as the witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from F ∩ G ≠ ∅ we existentially instantiate to get A0 ∈ F ∩ G, then use A0 as the witness for ∃A ∈ G(x ∈ A). Always consider how givens can produce the specific object you need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep scratch work separate from the final write-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Scratch work documents your planning, logical-form analysis, and the way you found witnesses; the final proof should present only the reasoning needed to justify the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process you used to discover a witness or a trick need not appear in the formal proof. Final proofs often omit the exploratory steps and may condense 'summing up' sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is acceptable to omit routine summations and small steps in final proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians often condense final proofs by skipping routine summing-up sentences and small algebraic/logical steps when knowledgeable readers can fill them in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers may need to fill in skipped steps; when learning, include more detail. The text comments that condensed summing-up sentences are common and that some steps (like choosing k = nm in a divisibility proof) are often omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with variable naming and scope to avoid ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing new variables (arbitrary or instantiated), ensure their scope and meaning are clear and do not conflict with existing names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always state whether a variable is arbitrary, a chosen witness, or a particular object from an existential given. Avoid implicit reuse that can lead to confusing or incorrect reasoning (see discussion on variable discipline in section).

rubrics_metrics.name: When using statements that begin with quantifiers, choose appropriate immediate actions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a given starting with ∃ apply existential instantiation immediately; for ∀ consider waiting until you have a particular element to substitute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existential givens are usually applied right away by naming a witness; universal givens are most useful after a suitable target value appears in the proof. This ordering prevents premature or unhelpful instantiation.
